results.title: Cross-channel attribution: what it shows and misses
results.markdown:
Title: Cross-channel attribution: what it shows and misses

URL Source: https://adwave.com/resources/cross-channel-attribution-measuring-tv

Published Time: 2026-10-17T00:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Cross-channel attribution splits credit for a conversion among the ads a customer touched on TV, search, social and the web. It shows which ads came before a sale but can’t prove which ones caused it. To learn what caused it, run an incrementality test, such as a holdout or geo experiment, which compares results with the ads and without them.

Cross-channel attribution is the practice of deciding how much credit each ad channel gets when a customer saw several of them before converting. With one channel the answer is simple. Once you run two or three, customers move between them, and someone has to decide how to split the sale.

Here’s an example. A homeowner sees a roofing company’s ad on a streaming TV app, and the name sticks. A few days later they scroll past the same company’s ad on Instagram. Two weeks after that, a storm hits. They search “roofer near me,” recognize the name in a Google ad, and click through to request a quote. Three channels touched that lead. Attribution is the set of rules that decides whether Google gets all the credit, whether TV gets some, or whether the credit is shared.

Those rules matter because your budget follows them. If your reports say search did all the work, you’ll move money into search. If TV planted the name that made the search click happen, that move can backfire. Our guide to [planning a multichannel approach](https://adwave.com/resources/multi-channel-marketing-approach) covers how channels fit together. This page is about how to read the credit.

## Why platform reports add up to more sales than you made

Every ad platform reports on its own contribution. Google’s dashboard measures Google, and Meta’s measures Facebook and Instagram. Each counts the conversions its ads touched, using its own conversion definition and attribution window. If a customer saw your Instagram ad and later clicked your Google ad, both platforms may claim the same sale.

![Image 1: Business owner at a kitchen table comparing stacks of printed reports with a calculator under warm lamp light](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/3cdaa9076dfd893672dd92d2d95f0f21f16a76d066d7e5a7eaff60ebf97029fa.jpg)

You can check this in about ten minutes:

1.   Pick one month.
2.   Write down the conversions or revenue each platform reports for that month.
3.   Add them up.
4.   Compare the total with your actual sales records.

If the platform total is well above your real total, the reports overlap. That doesn’t mean any platform is lying. It means none of them can see the others, so you can’t add their numbers together or treat any single one as the full picture. For context on how a campaign reaches people on search, social and video, see our [channels overview](https://adwave.com/channels).

## Common attribution models and what each one assumes

Every attribution model is a rule about who deserves credit. Each rule makes an assumption, and each assumption tilts results toward certain channels.

| Model | How it assigns credit | Good for | Known bias |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First-touch | All credit to the first ad the customer interacted with | Seeing which channels introduce new people to the business | Ignores everything that persuaded the customer afterward |
| Last-touch (last-click) | All credit to the final click or view before the conversion | Quick to set up and easy to read | Over-credits search and retargeting; can credit ads for sales that would have happened anyway |
| Multi-touch / data-driven | Splits credit across touchpoints, using either a fixed rule or a model trained on converting and non-converting paths | A fuller view of trackable digital journeys | Needs user-level tracking, so it can’t follow linear TV or other media it can’t tie to a person |

Last-touch is still widely used because it’s quick to set up and easy to read, even though it overvalues the final touchpoint and ignores everything that came before it, as the [Communications of the ACM guide to attribution](https://web.archive.org/web/20251029124135/https://cacm.acm.org/blogcacm/a-practical-guide-to-last-touch-and-multi-touch-attribution/) explains. Google has moved away from it as a default: in Google Ads, [Google’s attribution model documentation](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6259715?hl=en) says data-driven attribution is now the default for most conversion actions. In Google Analytics 4, [Google’s attribution reports guide](https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/10596866?hl=en) lists three models in its Attribution reports: data-driven attribution and two last-click models.

Data-driven attribution looks more complete, but it can only share credit among the touchpoints it can track. Media that can’t be tied to a person, such as linear TV, gets little or no credit.

## Why TV and connected TV get under-credited

Nobody clicks a TV ad. A streaming spot often works days or weeks later, when a viewer searches your name or types your web address. Search or direct traffic then collects the credit. The conversion also usually happens on a phone or laptop, a different device from the TV, which makes matching the two harder. Under last-touch, TV can create the demand and still appear to do nothing.

![Image 2: Homeowner on a couch watching streaming TV in the evening while holding a smartphone](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/f1c286b3dc5035484142108bc031767d49e4bc4ae02652bd434ee3a347488adc.jpg)

Some TV-to-web matching happens at the household level, but it covers only part of the journey. Our guide to [measuring CTV campaigns in detail](https://adwave.com/resources/ctv-measurement-attribution-guide) goes further into those methods.

Under-crediting is only half the risk. Attribution can also flatter a channel. Branded search and retargeting often reach people already on their way to buying, so they can claim sales they didn’t cause. Attribution can’t tell those two cases apart, which is why the next question matters.

## Attribution vs. incrementality

Attribution shows who converted after seeing an ad. Incrementality shows who converted because of the ad.

![Image 3: Two similar small-town main streets in daylight, one busy with shoppers and the other quiet](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/1c01751feaa6b9fd8d621d44bbd8028a8f812777dd0ace5e646d84832cbe4f39.jpg)

An incrementality test works like a controlled experiment. You show ads to one group (a set of people or a set of geographic markets) and hold them back from a similar group. The difference in sales between the treatment and holdout groups is the lift the ads caused. In a geo test, you turn off spend in some markets and keep it running in others. Streaming TV suits this because most streaming platforms support geographic targeting exclusions.

| Method | Question it answers | Strength | Tradeoff |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Attribution | Which ads came before conversions? | Fast and frequent, good for day-to-day changes | Not causal; depends on what can be tracked |
| Media mix modeling | How have spend and sales moved together over time? | Broad view for budget planning | Correlation-based; needs a long data history |
| Incrementality testing | How many sales did these ads cause? | Causal, and reaches non-clickable media like TV | Slower; needs a large enough budget and a long enough run to produce a clear result |

Tests have costs. The held-back market sees no ads while the test runs, and a test typically takes several weeks, long enough to cover the lag between seeing an ad and buying. In one geo holdout on streaming TV by [Measured’s incrementality research](https://www.measured.com/faq/how-to-measure-tv-ctv-incrementality/), roughly half of the conversions the ad platform had claimed were actually incremental. A test’s result can be higher or lower than what your dashboards show.

## How a small business can measure TV, search and social together

You don’t need an analytics team to measure honestly. Here’s a workable process:

1.   Install tracking on your website and count only the actions that matter to the business, whether that’s a call, a booking, or a purchase.
2.   Give each conversion a value. A rough average job value lets you compare revenue against spend instead of only counting clicks.
3.   Read last-touch and assisted conversions side by side. Last-touch shows who closed the sale; assisted conversions show which channels appeared earlier. A channel with few last-touch sales and many assists is probably doing early work.
4.   Watch branded search and direct traffic around any change to your TV campaign. A rise in people searching your name is a signal, not proof.
5.   Test the channel you doubt most. Run a geo or holdout test long enough to cover your normal sales cycle. Our guide to [

results.title: Bringing clarity to Connected TV attribution: Techniques and innovations
results.markdown:
Title: Bringing clarity to Connected TV attribution: Techniques and innovations

URL Source: https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/connected-tv-attribution

Published Time: 2025-02-06T11:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
As [connected TV (CTV)](https://www.stackadapt.com/connected-tv-advertising) continues to grow as a dominant force in advertising, it offers brands unparalleled opportunities to engage audiences in more targeted and impactful ways. Yet, one critical question lingers: _How do we measure the real impact of CTV campaigns?_

[Measurement](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/ctv-measurement) and [attribution](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/what-is-marketing-attribution) are among the most crucial—and challenging—frontiers in unlocking the full potential of CTV advertising. According to recent data, advertisers are aware of this, with [86% prioritizing reach and frequency](https://chart-na1.emarketer.com/268178/importance-of-select-reporting-metrics-connected-tv-ctvott-advertising-according-us-ctvott-advertisers-april-2024-of-respondents) and 85% emphasizing [brand lift](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/stackadapt-brand-lift-study) as important reporting metrics. However, metrics like sales lift (84%) and website visit attribution (77%) illustrate a growing focus on connecting campaign performance to tangible business outcomes.

This article explores how new tools and techniques tackle these challenges head-on. From tracking cross-device activity to connecting online impressions with offline actions, we’ll unpack the strategies that will help you prove the value of your campaigns and optimize them for greater impact.

## Understanding CTV attribution

CTV attribution refers to the process of determining how [CTV advertising](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/integrate-connected-tv) campaigns influence consumer actions and contribute to business outcomes. It bridges the gap between ad exposure and measurable results, such as website visits, app downloads, or in-store purchases.

Unlike [traditional TV advertising](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/linear-tv-vs-connected-tv), which often relies on broad audience metrics, CTV attribution allows advertisers to track more specific behaviours, connecting the dots between an ad and its impact on the bottom line.

CTV attribution typically involves collecting data from various sources to create a clear picture of viewer interactions. This includes tracking ad impressions on CTV devices, integrating [1st-](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/1st-party-data) and [3rd-party data](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/third-party-audiences), and analyzing user actions across multiple channels and devices.

For example, if a consumer sees a CTV ad and later visits the advertiser’s website or completes a purchase, attribution models can link those actions back to the original ad exposure.

Advanced tools often use household-level data, cross-device tracking, and machine learning to refine the accuracy of these insights.

Focusing on attribution is essential because it helps advertisers understand the actual value of their campaigns. CTV’s ability to target specific audiences makes it a highly efficient advertising channel, but without proper attribution, businesses may struggle to justify their investments.

Demonstrating a clear connection between ad exposure and [key performance indicators (KPIs)](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/programmatic-kpis-explained) such as sales or engagement builds confidence in the channel’s effectiveness. Additionally, robust attribution allows advertisers to optimize their [CTV strategies](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/connected-tv-marketing-strategies) by identifying which campaigns, creatives, or placements drive the most impact, leading to more informed decisions and better returns on ad spend.

## Attribution models for Connected TV

Understanding the different attribution models used in CTV advertising is key to evaluating campaign performance and making data-driven decisions. Each model approaches the question of “what led to the conversion?” differently, offering distinct benefits and limitations.

### First-touch attribution

This model gives 100% credit to a viewer’s first interaction with a CTV ad or campaign. For example, if a consumer sees a brand’s CTV ad and later visits its website after other touchpoints like social media or email, the CTV ad is considered solely responsible for driving the conversion.

*   **Strengths**: Ideal for understanding which campaigns generate initial interest and awareness. It’s simple to implement and provides clear insights into top-of-funnel performance.
*   **Weaknesses**: Ignores the influence of subsequent interactions that may have contributed to the final conversion, leading to an incomplete picture of the customer journey.

### Last-touch attribution

This model attributes 100% of the credit to the final interaction before the conversion. For instance, if a consumer sees a CTV ad, clicks on a paid search ad days later, and completes a purchase, the search ad would receive full credit.

*   **Strengths**: Highlights the last step in the conversion funnel, helping advertisers understand which touchpoint directly drives actions like purchases or sign-ups.
*   **Weaknesses**: Oversimplifies the journey by disregarding earlier touchpoints, potentially undervaluing the role of CTV in building awareness and nurturing interest.

### Multi-touch attribution

Multi-touch attribution spreads credit across all touchpoints in a consumer’s journey. For example, if a viewer sees a CTV ad, clicks on a social media ad, and finally receives an email prompting the purchase, each interaction is assigned a proportionate share of credit.

*   **Strengths**: Provides a holistic view of how various touchpoints work together, making it easier to optimize cross-channel campaigns. It’s particularly useful in complex, [multi-channel advertising strategies](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/downloads/guide-to-multi-channel-advertising).
*   **Weaknesses**: It can be challenging to implement due to its reliance on robust data collection and sophisticated modelling. Assigning weights to each touchpoint can also be subjective.

### View-through attribution

This model credits a conversion to a CTV ad even if the consumer did not click on it, as long as they were exposed to it and later completed the desired action. For example, if someone sees a CTV ad for a fitness brand and buys a product online days later without clicking a direct link, the view-through model credits the ad exposure.

*   **Strengths**: Captures the impact of passive exposure, which is critical for CTV campaigns that don’t rely on direct clicks. It reflects how top-of-funnel activity influences conversions.
*   **Weaknesses**: Correlation doesn’t always mean causation; unrelated factors could have influenced the conversion, making it harder to prove a direct connection.

### The micro-conversion revolution

While traditional attribution focuses on the final conversion (e.g., a purchase), the micro-conversion revolution emphasizes smaller, incremental actions that indicate progress along the customer journey. Micro-conversions include visiting a landing page, adding a product to a cart, or signing up for a newsletter after viewing a CTV ad. These micro-actions provide richer insights into consumer behaviour and how CTV ads move prospects closer to the ultimate conversion.

This approach is gaining traction because it enables advertisers to optimize campaigns in real time by identifying and focusing on high-value touchpoints earlier in the funnel.

Selecting the right attribution model often depends on the campaign’s goals and the available data. A combination of models tailored to specific objectives can help advertisers get the most comprehensive view of their CTV campaign performance.

## Benefits and advantages of CTV attribution

CTV attribution provides advertisers the tools to bridge the gap between ad exposure and measurable business outcomes. Below are the key advantages of implementing a robust CTV attribution approach.

### Accurate attribution for performance clarity

Attribution frameworks help establish a clear link between CTV ad exposure and online engagement. Rather than relying on traditional TV metrics, advertisers can track how CTV influences website visits, conversions, and other key actions. This level of accuracy ensures a more precise understanding of campaign impact.

### Enhanced tracking across devices

With consumers engaging across multiple screens, cross-device tracking is essential. Advanced identity resolution technology connects CTV impressions to user actions across mobile, desktop, and other devices. This ensures a more complete and unified view of the customer journey.

### Optimized campaign performance

results.title: CTV measurement: Metrics & KPIs you should track to prove performance
results.markdown:
Title: CTV measurement: Metrics & KPIs you should track to prove performance

URL Source: https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/ctv-measurement

Published Time: 2025-01-22T14:04:16+00:00

Markdown Content:
For years, advertisers prioritized [traditional linear TV advertising](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/linear-tv-vs-connected-tv) over other channels for its broad reach and affordability.

There was just one major problem: reporting was limited, with advertisers often relying on estimated viewership numbers from Nielsen ratings and spikes in web or store traffic after a commercial aired to assess whether a campaign was effective.

[Connected TV (CTV) advertising](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/integrate-connected-tv) changes that.

With CTV measurement, marketers can access accurate, granular insights to adjust, optimize, and personalize campaigns for better performance, in real time and throughout the entire funnel.

CTV’s advanced measurement capabilities are part of the reason why CTV advertising continues experiencing [historic adoption](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/connected-tv-stats), with CTV ad spending forecasted to see [double-digit annual growth](https://content-na1.emarketer.com/one-of-largest-sources-of-new-video-ad-inventory-spending-ctv) and reach $46.89 billion USD in 2028, the same year EMARKETER predicts it will officially surpass traditional linear TV ad spending.

With CTV expected to account for [20%](https://content-na1.emarketer.com/4-ctv-ad-spend-trends-track-2025) of the average US adult’s media time per day by 2026, it’s never been more clear that CTV is [the future of TV advertising](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/future-of-connected-tv).

Read on to learn how CTV measurement works, what metrics and KPIs you need to track, and how you can use it to go beyond top-of-funnel awareness and increase conversions for you or your clients.

## What is Connected TV measurement?

CTV measurement tracks and analyzes the performance of CTV ad campaigns, providing marketers with the data needed to optimize and assess the effectiveness of their [CTV marketing strategies](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/connected-tv-marketing-strategies).

## How does CTV measurement work?

Here’s a simplified explanation of how CTV measurement works and can be used to [improve attribution and campaign performance](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/tips-for-successful-ctv-advertising-campaigns):

*   Similar to the measurement methods used for display ads or other forms of digital advertising, a 1×1 pixel is placed on the [CTV creative](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/ctv-creative-best-practices) and the advertiser’s landing page.
*   The client works with the [CTV advertising platform](https://www.stackadapt.com/connected-tv-advertising) to define the conditions that trigger when the pixel events fire (for example, based on a view-through or quartile completion).
*   CTV ads are then served to targeted audiences through the platform based on the campaign parameters.
*   When a viewer sees an ad or takes an action that triggers the pixel event to fire, the signal is sent back to the platform’s pixel server to record the event and measure the performance of the CTV campaign. For example, if a user watches a CTV ad in full and visits the advertiser’s landing page within a predefined timeframe to make a purchase, a view-through conversion is recorded, attributing the action to the CTV campaign.
*   Advertisers can then use these insights to optimize and further refine their CTV campaigns, providing them with actionable data to improve performance and demonstrate ROI to key stakeholders or clients.

Of course, CTV measurement doesn’t only apply to online conversions. As we’ll get into later, it can also be used with tools and 3rd-party integrations to assess more than online sales, such as increased brand awareness or [foot traffic](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/footfall-attribution).

## 9 CTV metrics you need to track

There are various sets of CTV metrics and KPIs that you can use to assess the success of your ads. Ultimately, the ones you choose should be based on the unique goals of your campaign.

To help you get started, here are some common ones you should consider tracking:

### 1. Impressions

Impressions track how many times a CTV ad is shown to viewers. This simple metric—a foundational element of [reporting in digital advertising](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/programmatic-kpis-explained)—is a huge improvement over traditional TV measurement, providing a clearer picture of ad delivery and audience reach.

### 2. Frequency

Frequency measures how many times a unique viewer sees your ad. In CTV advertising, maintaining the right frequency is critical: too few exposures may fail to build awareness, while too many can lead to [ad fatigue](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/ad-fatigue). Leveraging in-platform tools, like frequency caps, helps you strike the ideal balance—maximizing awareness and recall without overwhelming viewers.

### 3. Cost per mille (CPM)

CPM is a valuable metric, particularly in CTV advertising, because it allows advertisers to calculate the cost of delivering 1,000 ad impressions on various CTV platforms, helping them allocate budgets and plan their campaigns more effectively.

CPMs are typically higher in CTV than in other forms of digital advertising, with rates often ranging from [$15 to $30 USD](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/ctv-b2b-advertising#myths). That’s because CTV offers [premium inventory](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/connected-tv-inventory) compared to traditional digital video, with advertisers able to place ads on [Disney+](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/stackadapt-fuels-advertising-growth-disney-ctv), [Channel 4](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/channel-4), and [other high-profile publishers](https://www.stackadapt.com/connected-tv-advertising).

### 4. Unique households

To measure the number of unique viewers exposed to your CTV ad, it’s important to focus on the unique number of households you reach. That’s because each household represents a distinct viewing environment, typically associated with a specific IP address, that could have multiple users streaming content and seeing the same ad together at the same time, making tracking unique households a more accurate metric in terms of measuring reach than individual impressions alone.

### 5. Completion rate

The completion rate measures how much your CTV ad users watch from start to finish. Completion rates are typically higher in CTV than in [other forms of video advertising](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1412252/frequency-skip-in-app-ad/) because ads on CTV platforms are generally unskippable. Still, the completion rate is worth monitoring to assess audience engagement and the effectiveness of different ad creatives.

### 6. Cost per completed view (CPCV)

CPCV measures the amount an advertiser pays to a CTV platform or ad inventory provider when an ad is viewed through to completion. This pricing model ensures that advertisers pay exclusively for completed views. CPCV is particularly effective in CTV because, as previously mentioned, unskippable ads contribute to higher completion rates and provide better value for advertisers.

### 7. Return on ad spend (ROAS)

ROAS measures the revenue earned for every dollar spent on CTV advertising. Similar to return on investment (ROI), ROAS measures the ROI of the money that was invested into a CTV campaign, helping you understand the effectiveness your campaign has on driving revenue and achieving your campaign goals.

### 8. View-through conversions

This metric measures how many people converted (for example, visited your website and made a purchase within a specific period of time) after viewing your CTV ad. Since CTV ads typically lack direct clicks, this metric highlights a CTV ad’s impact on driving conversions through indirect paths, supplementing [traditional click-through metrics](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/view-through-click-through-conversions) and providing actionable insights into brand recall and campaign effectiveness.

### 9. Conversion rate

The conversion rate measures what percentage of viewers took a specific action—for example, visiting an [e-commerce](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/ecommerce-advertising-strategies) site and making a purchase—after seeing your CTV ad campaign. This is calculated by dividing the total number of CTV-certified conversions by the total number of CTV-certified visits and multiplying by 100 to arrive at the conversion percentage.

Another strategy for CTV measurement is to leverage a [brand lift study](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/stackadapt-brand-lift-study).

Adding these events to your website or mobile app helps you measure additional features and behavior as well as generate more useful reports, and build [suggested audiences](https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/10427338). Because these events require additional context to be meaningful, they're not sent automatically.

Use the links in this article to see the prescribed parameters for each event. You should send recommended events with their prescribed parameters to get the most details in your reports and to benefit from future features and integrations as they become available.

To learn how to set up a recommended event on your website, see [Set up events](https://developers.google.com/analytics/devguides/collection/ga4/events). For your app project, see [Log events](https://firebase.google.com/docs/analytics/events?platform=ios).The data from these events automatically update predefined dimensions and metrics so you can analyze the data in your reports.

## [](https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9267735)For all properties

We recommend these events to all customers in all business verticals. Later sections in this article include some of these events when we recommend sending the events for the given use case.

| --- | --- |

Title: Connected TV Attribution & Incrementality: Complete Measurement Guide for DTC Brands

URL Source: https://www.attnagency.com/blog/ctv-attribution-incrementality

Markdown Content:
## Connected TV Attribution & Incrementality: Complete Measurement Guide for DTC Brands

Connected TV advertising presents unique measurement challenges that traditional digital attribution methods can't solve. For DTC brands investing $50K+ monthly in CTV, proving incrementality and understanding true attribution is critical for scaling campaigns profitably.

This comprehensive guide covers advanced CTV measurement strategies, incrementality testing methodologies, and attribution frameworks based on $75M+ in annual CTV spend across 200+ DTC campaigns.

## The CTV Attribution Challenge

Connected TV operates fundamentally differently from click-based digital advertising, creating unique measurement challenges:

### Why Traditional Attribution Fails

**No Click-Through Tracking:**

*   CTV ads can't be clicked like search or social ads
*   Traditional last-click attribution completely misses CTV impact
*   View-through windows become critical for measurement

**Cross-Device User Journey:**

*   Viewers see CTV ads on smart TVs
*   Actions often happen on mobile devices or computers
*   Identity resolution across devices becomes essential

**Long Attribution Windows:**

*   CTV impact can take days or weeks to materialize
*   Traditional 1-day attribution windows miss most conversions
*   Need for extended attribution periods (14-30+ days)

### The Measurement Gap Problem

**Undervaluation of CTV:**

*   Platform reporting often shows 40-70% lower conversions than reality
*   Budget gets allocated to "easier to measure" channels
*   CTV campaigns get paused prematurely due to perceived poor performance

**Incrementality Questions:**

*   Were these customers going to convert anyway?
*   How much additional revenue is CTV actually driving?
*   What's the true ROI when accounting for baseline sales?

## Foundation: CTV Tracking Setup

### Technical Infrastructure Requirements

**Device Identification:**

*   **Connected TV Device IDs:** Samsung, Roku, LG, etc.
*   **IP Address Matching:** Household-level identification
*   **Mobile Advertising IDs:** Cross-device connection
*   **First-Party Data Integration:** Customer database matching

**Tracking Technology Stack:**

*   **Conversion APIs:** Server-side tracking for privacy compliance
*   **Customer Data Platforms:** Unified customer profiles
*   **Marketing Mix Modeling:** Statistical attribution analysis
*   **Incrementality Testing Platforms:** Controlled experiment design

### Platform-Specific Setup

**The Trade Desk:**

*   Implement Unified ID 2.0 for enhanced targeting
*   Setup household-level conversion tracking
*   Configure extended attribution windows (14-30 days)
*   Enable cross-device reporting

**Samsung Ads:**

*   Activate Samsung's device graph for cross-screen attribution
*   Setup household reach and frequency measurement
*   Implement deterministic device matching
*   Enable first-party data onboarding

**Roku Advertising:**

*   Configure Roku's measurement partner integrations
*   Setup streaming reach and frequency reporting
*   Implement household conversion tracking
*   Enable cross-platform attribution

## Advanced Attribution Methodologies

### 1. Multi-Touch Attribution (MTA)

**Implementation Framework:**

**Data Collection:**

*   Track all customer touchpoints across channels
*   Capture CTV exposure data with timestamps
*   Record conversion events with full customer journey
*   Integrate offline conversion data

**Attribution Modeling:**

*   **Time-Decay Model:** Give more credit to recent touchpoints
*   **Position-Based Model:** Credit first and last touches heavily
*   **Data-Driven Model:** Use machine learning for credit assignment
*   **Shapley Value Model:** Game theory approach to credit distribution

**Practical Setup:**

```
Attribution Window Configuration:
- CTV View-Through: 14-30 days
- Display: 7 days view, 1 day click
- Social: 7 days view, 1 day click  
- Search: 30 days click
- Email: 3 days click
```

### 2. Marketing Mix Modeling (MMM)

**Why MMM for CTV:**

*   Accounts for baseline sales and market factors
*   Measures true incrementality across all channels
*   Handles complex interaction effects between media
*   Provides forward-looking optimization insights

**Data Requirements:**

*   **Daily sales data** for 2+ years
*   **Media spend data** across all channels
*   **External factors:** Seasonality, pricing, promotions, weather
*   **Competitive activity:** Competitor advertising levels

**Model Development Process:**

**Week 1-2: Data Collection and Preparation**

*   Gather historical sales and marketing data
*   Clean and normalize data across sources
*   Create external variable datasets
*   Establish baseline sales periods

**Week 3-4: Model Building**

*   Define adstock and saturation parameters
*   Test various model structures
*   Validate against holdout periods
*   Calibrate with incrementality test results

**Week 5-6: Analysis and Insights**

*   Calculate channel-specific ROI and incrementality
*   Identify optimal budget allocation
*   Forecast impact of budget changes
*   Develop scenario planning models

### 3. Geo-Holdout Testing

**Methodology Overview:** Split geographic markets into test and control groups to measure true CTV incrementality.

**Test Design Framework:**

**Market Selection:**

*   Choose 20+ matched market pairs
*   Balance markets by size, demographics, seasonality
*   Ensure sufficient statistical power (typically need $100K+ monthly spend)
*   Account for geographic spillover effects

**Test Setup:**

```
Test Group: Normal CTV campaign execution
Control Group: CTV advertising paused or reduced by 50-80%
Duration: 6-12 weeks minimum for statistical significance
Measurement: Compare sales lift between groups
```

**Statistical Analysis:**

*   Calculate incremental sales lift percentage
*   Determine statistical significance (p-value <0.05)
*   Account for market-level confounding variables
*   Calculate incremental ROAS and payback period

## Incrementality Testing Strategies

### 1. Ghost Ads Methodology

**How It Works:** Serve "ghost" impressions to control group users who would have seen CTV ads but without actually showing the creative.

**Implementation:**

*   Use platforms that support ghost ad serving (The Trade Desk, Samsung)
*   Randomly assign households to test/control groups
*   Track conversion behavior across both groups
*   Measure incremental lift from actual ad exposure

**Advantages:**

*   Perfect user-level matching between test and control
*   Eliminates geographic spillover effects
*   Provides highly accurate incrementality measurement
*   Can run continuously for ongoing optimization

### 2. Daypart-Based Testing

**Strategy:** Test different CTV dayparts against control periods to understand optimal timing and incrementality.

**Test Structure:**

```
Test Periods:
- Prime Time (7-11 PM): Full CTV spend
- Late Night (11 PM-1 AM): 50% spend reduction  
- Morning (6-9 AM): Complete pause
- Control Comparison: Previous months same dayparts
```

**Measurement Focus:**

*   Conversion rate differences by exposed daypart
*   Cost per acquisition variations
*   Long-term customer value by acquisition time
*   Cross-device conversion timing patterns

### 3. Audience Segment Testing

**Methodology:** Create matched audience segments with varying CTV exposure levels to measure incremental impact.

**Segment Design:**

*   **Heavy Exposure:** 8+ impressions per person per week
*   **Medium Exposure:** 4-7 impressions per person per week
*   **Light Exposure:** 1-3 impressions per person per week
*   **Control:** No CTV exposure but similar demographic profile

**Analysis Framework:**

*   Plot conversion rates vs. exposure levels
*   Calculate optimal frequency for maximum incrementality
*   Identify diminishing returns thresholds
*   Optimize campaign reach vs. frequency balance

## Attribution Windows and Time-Decay

### Optimal Attribution Window Setting

**Industry Benchmarks by Vertical:**

**Beauty/Skincare:**

*   Primary window: 14 days
*   Extended window: 28 days (captures 85%+ of conversions)
*   Time-decay half-life: 3-4 days

**Apparel:**

*   Primary window: 21 days
*   Extended window: 45 days (seasonal considerations)
*   Time-decay half-life: 5-7 days

**Home/Garden:**

*   Primary window: 30 days
*   Extended window: 60 days (higher consideration purchase)
*   Time-decay half-life: 7-10 days

### Time-Decay Models

**Linear Time-Decay:** Equal reduction in attribution value over time

```
Day 1: 100% attribution value
Day 7: 50% attribution value
Day 14: 0% attribution value
```

**Exponential Time-Decay:** Rapid decline in attribution value

```
Day 1: 100% attribution value
Day 3: 50% attribution value  
Day 7: 25% attribution value
Day 14: 12.5% attribution
